paras: The expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph was the beating and driving out of a Black schoolteacher by a mob in Raleigh County, West Virginia, reported in February 1882. According to Randolph's own statement, the mob beat him and ordered him to leave after a justice acquitted men he had had arrested, and he left to save his life. A Parkersburg paper headed its notice of the case "SHAMEFUL" while qualifying its comment on whether the statement was true.

Randolph, described as "a colored school teacher of Raleigh county," taught at a school in the county. In his account, a mob subjected him to abuse and threats in an effort to drive him from his school and from the community. No reason for the campaign against him is given in the coverage, and neither the date nor the location of the school is named.

Randolph responded to the threats by having some of the parties arrested for their abuse. The case went before a justice, who acquitted them, in Randolph's words "unjustly." After the acquittal, the mob beat Randolph and ordered him to leave, and he did so, as he put it, "to save his life."

Randolph made his experience public in a statement printed by the Charleston Leader. No report of arrests or prosecution for the beating, or of any action by county authorities, was found in the coverage.

The case is known from a single paragraph in the "West Virginia Notes" column of the West Virginia Freeman of Parkersburg on February 22, 1882, which summarized Randolph's statement from the Charleston Leader. Under the heading "SHAMEFUL," the Freeman described the mob's "most disgraceful proceedings" but hedged with "If these are facts." It closed by predicting that "the good people of Raleigh county" would apply "a vigorous remedy," without saying what that remedy should be.
The item ran between paragraphs on temperance and local prohibition, and the original Leader statement does not appear in the coverage.
